Issued at 221 AM EDT Wed Sep 2 2026

Today-Tonight...Portions of this discussion are getting a bit 
repetitive (some parts even copy-pasted), but as long as the local
pattern is dominated by high moisture in onshore flow, we'll 
continue to keep seeing the same conditions day to day. Ridging 
aloft has settled over the southeastern US, flattened by a low 
pressure system tracking across southeast Canada, and between 
troughs/low pressure systems over the west coast and western 
Atlantic. The ridge remains far enough north disturbances 
transiting the southern flank will pass above Florida and the 
Gulf. At the surface the ridge axis of the Bermuda high continues 
its residency north of Florida, and low pressure systems to the 
north and an inverted trough entering the local Atlantic waters 
have weakened/shifted the pressure gradient. Low-level flow 
remains onshore, but will vary between northeasterly and 
southeasterly as the trough approaches and moves inland. 
Anomalously high moisture will accompany the trough, keeping rain 
chances well above normal. We'll continue the pattern of isolated 
to scattered showers developing over the Atlantic waters in the 
early morning, some of which may move onshore, then additional 
scattered to numerous showers will develop inland/near the coast 
in the late morning to early afternoon, pushing inland with a 
quick/diffuse east coast sea breeze through the rest of the 
afternoon and early evening. While subsidence behind the sea 
breeze should knock down coverage east the boundary, the multiple 
disturbances and lurking outflow boundaries could fire off 
additional rounds of convection at any point. So far the trough 
hasn't kicked up much more convection than we've seen previous 
days/nights, but should some upper-level support swing through at 
the right time there could be flare up leading to training of 
heavy rainfall along the coast from the Cape north, and wider 
coverage of showers and storms elsewhere.

Model and upper air soundings continue to show a nearly saturated
environment (PWATs 2.2-2.4", up to 2.5" in convection) with long-
skinny instability profiles (CAPE generally 1,000-2,000 J/kg, 
though some surface based parcels could push towards 3,000 J/kg) 
and warm mid-levels (T500 -5C to -4C) characteristic of heavy 
rainfall. Weak easterly steering flow will gradually usher showers
and storms towards the west side of the peninsula and a sea breeze
collision over there, but varying low-level flow and chaotic 
boundary interactions could cause erratic storm motion. Storms or 
heavy showers that become slow or hung up on boundaries could 
produce a quick 2-3" of rainfall leading to ponding of water on 
roads and minor flooding of urban, low-lying, or poor drainage 
areas. There is a very low (up to 5%) chance for one or two spots 
to receive +4" of rainfall leading to greater flooding impacts, 
and the Weather Prediction Center has outlooked all of East 
Central Florida in a Marginal (level 1 of 4) risk for excessive 
rainfall. In addition to the rainfall, stronger storms and heavy 
showers will be capable of gusty winds to around 45 mph from 
water loading. Occasional to frequent cloud to ground lightning 
will accompany thunderstorms. 

As for the rest of the forecast, lots of cloud cover keeps 
temperatures seasonable with highs in the U80s-L90s, and lows in 
the 70s. Peak afternoon heat indices 98-106. Be sure to take 
frequent breaks in the shade or air conditioning if spending 
prolonged time outdoors to avoid the development of heat-related 
illness. Incoming swell from back when Dolly reached tropical 
storm strength has arrived at the Volusia and Northern Brevard 
coasts (NOAA buoys 41009 and 41010 showing swell periods up to 13s
from the ESE-SE) and a High risk of dangerous rip currents has 
been issued for these beaches. The Bahamas has provided some 
shelter from this long period swell to the Treasure and Southern 
Brevard beaches, where a Moderate risk of rip currents continues. 
Will being monitoring these beaches, and may need to upgrade the 
risk if conditions warrant. 

Thursday-Friday...A little bit of forecast uncertainty, mainly 
Friday. The low pressure system in southeastern Canada deepens 
while sliding towards New England and the Canadian Maritimes, 
amplifying the pattern over the CONUS and causing the mid-upper 
level ridge over the Southeast to quickly slither back into the 
Central US. The western periphery of the Bermuda high will 
further weaken as the the surface ridge axis begins to drop 
towards Florida. Low-level flow technically remains onshore, but 
becomes southeasterly Thursday and southerly Friday. A second, 
very weak surface trough looks to develop near the coast Thursday,
which will reinforce the high moisture, then there could be some 
dry air intrusion to the south Friday according to the GFS, but 
the ECM currently doesn't agree. There's also some disagreement on
